In terms of lexical stress and vowel distribution, on the other hand, there is not much difference between the three dialects. ... In the Waigeo dialects, if such words [words that have penultimate stress] have the same vowel in penultimate and final syllables, and end in an open syllable, the final syllable vowel is apocopated when the word appears in sentence-medial context. ... [6.4.3] I. If a polysyllabic word has a vowel other than /a/ in the penultimate syllable, it can only have penultimate stress. sources.citation: Arnold, Laura. 2026. Sketch grammars of Wauyai Maˈya and Batta: Two undocumented Austronesian languages of Raja Ampat, northwest New Guinea. Language Documentation & Conservation 20: 1-51. hdl.handle.net/10125/74842
sources.quote: "As first noted by Remijsen (2001a; 2001b), Wauyai also has an orthogonal system of contrastive stress: in the majority of words, either the penultimate or final syllable of a word bears stress. Perceptual correlates of stress are a greater intensity, longer vowel duration, and falling pitch. Words with penultimate stress cannot bear Rise tone." Minimal pairs: ˈmɐnɐ³ 'light (weight)' vs mɐˈnɐ³ 'animal fat' vs mɐˈnɐ¹² 'mucus'; ˈɐnɐ 'thing'. sources.note: Only Wauyai-specific description (2019/2023 fieldwork, F0 plots, stress minimal pairs); confirms our lexical penult/final stress coding but overturns the record's tone_note (Wauyai IS tonal, contra Remijsen 2001) and adds the co-occurrence restriction 'penultimate stress cannot bear Rise tone'. Should be cited alongside Remijsen 2001.

sources.quote: "The word prosodic systems of the Maˈya dialects (Kawe, Laganyan, Wauyai, Salawati, Misool) and Biga are all very similar ... all these varieties are analysed with both lexical tone and lexical stress. ... Stress, on the other hand, falls unpredictably on either the penultimate or final syllable of polysyllabic words in all varieties"; fn.12: "Remijsen (2001a: 21, 2001b) analyses Kawe Maˈya and Wauyai Maˈya as atonal. Data collected for this project, however, provides evidence for tone in both varieties ... see Arnold (forthc.) on tone in Wauyai Maˈya."

sources.note: Ma'ya has three lexically contrastive tonemes (High, Rise, Fall); accounts of the Misool, Salawati and Laganyan dialect tone systems and their diachrony (Rise most variable; Misool push-chain shift of Fall; Laganyan loses the Fall/Rise contrast in one context and has a boundary tone surfacing with voiced codas). For Wauyai itself it classes the dialect as lacking lexical tone (per Arnold 2025 fn.12, 2026 p.5) - the analysis Arnold 2026 overturns.

tone.summary: Ma'ya: 3 tonemes H, Rise, Fall (Remijsen); Wauyai analysed as atonal here, contra Arnold 2026.
